question: Water is rising in my street right now and starting to come into the yard. What do I do?
answer: Get to safety now. If officials have told you to evacuate, leave immediately; otherwise move to higher ground or to a higher floor. Do not walk, swim or drive through flood water: just six inches of moving water can knock you down and one foot of moving water can sweep a vehicle away. Turn around, don't drown, never drive around barricades and stay off bridges over fast-moving water. If you are trapped in the building, go to the highest level, but do not climb into a closed attic where rising water can trap you; get on the roof only if necessary and signal for help from there. Keep listening to EAS, NOAA Weather Radio or local alerts for instructions, and call 9-1-1 if someone has a medical emergency.

question: My car stalled on a flooded road, the water is moving fast and coming in under the doors. What should I do?
answer: Do not step out into the current. If your car is trapped in rapidly moving water, stay inside it; if the water is rising inside the car, climb out onto the roof and stay there. Moving water is far stronger than it looks: six inches of it can knock a person down, and one foot can sweep a vehicle away; a foot of water will float many cars. So do not try to wade or swim to the bank and do not try to drive on through it. From the roof, signal for help. For next time: never drive through flooded roads or around barricades. Turn around, don't drown.

question: The building is shaking right now, earthquake! I'm inside at my desk, do I run out?
answer: Do not run outside. Drop, Cover and Hold On right where you are. Drop onto your hands and knees. Cover your head and neck with one arm and hand and crawl under your desk if it is sturdy; if there is no shelter nearby, crawl next to an interior wall away from windows, stay on your knees and bend over to protect vital organs. Hold On until the shaking stops: if you are under the desk, hold it with one hand and be ready to move with it. Avoid doorways. When the shaking stops, expect aftershocks and drop, cover and hold on again if one comes. If the building is damaged, go outside and move quickly away from it.

question: Earthquake is over but I'm pinned under part of a fallen wall, I can move my arms and I have my phone. How do I get help?
answer: Signal, don't shout. Send a text message with where you are; texts may get through when calls do not and they save battery. Bang on a pipe or wall so rescuers can hear you, and if you have a whistle, use it instead of shouting. Cover your mouth with your shirt to protect yourself from dust. Do not try to remove heavy debris by yourself, and expect aftershocks: protect your head and neck with your arms if the ground shakes again. Keep your phone use to texts to save power, and keep signalling at intervals until help arrives.

question: Tornado warning just went off and I live in an apartment with no basement. Where do I go?
answer: Move now. Go to a small, interior, windowless room on the lowest level of your building, such as an inner bathroom, closet or hallway on the ground floor; if your building has a storm shelter or safe room, or you cannot stay at home, use that or a public shelter. Stay away from windows, doors and outside walls. Get down, cover your head and neck with your arms, and pull furniture, a mattress or blankets around or on top of you for protection from flying debris, which causes most injuries and deaths. Keep listening to EAS, NOAA Weather Radio or local alerts and stay put until officials say the danger has passed.

question: I'm driving and I can see a tornado. Should I get under that highway overpass up ahead?
answer: No. Do not shelter under the overpass: bridges create deadly traffic hazards and offer little protection from flying debris. There is no safe option in a car, only less dangerous ones. If the tornado is visible, far away and traffic is light, you may be able to drive out of its path by moving at right angles to it. If you are caught by extreme winds or flying debris, park as quickly and safely as possible out of the traffic lanes, stay in the car with your seat belt on, put your head down below the windows and cover your head with your hands and a coat or blanket. If you can safely get noticeably lower than the roadway, leave the car, lie down there and cover your head with your hands.

question: Storm surge from the hurricane is flooding our house and we didn't get out in time. Should we go up into the attic?
answer: Go up, but not into a closed attic. Move everyone to the highest level of the building; a closed attic can become a trap if the water keeps rising, because you may not be able to get out. If the water keeps rising and you must, get on the roof and signal for help from there. Do not try to walk, swim or drive out through the flood water: storm surge is historically the leading cause of hurricane deaths in the United States, and just six inches of fast-moving water can knock you down. Keep paying attention to emergency alerts and instructions. Once the storm passes, do not wade in flood water, which can carry debris, chemicals and live electrical current.

question: There was a big earthquake a few minutes ago and now the ocean is pulling way back from the beach. What do I do?
answer: Leave the beach right now and get to high ground as far inland as possible. A strong earthquake followed by the ocean suddenly draining is a natural warning sign of a tsunami; do not wait for an official warning or evacuation order. Aim for ground 100 feet or more above sea level, or at least one mile inland, and follow evacuation-route signs, which show a wave with an arrow pointing toward higher ground. If you end up in the water, grab onto something that floats. Tsunamis are a series of waves, so stay on high ground and listen to local alerts until authorities say it is safe to return.

question: The wildfire cut off our road and we can't evacuate. Smoke is getting into the house. What do we do?
answer: Call 9-1-1 now and give your exact location, and tell them you are trapped; be aware that response could be delayed or impossible, so keep protecting yourselves. Turn on lights so rescuers can find you. Limit the smoke: close all doors and windows, pick one room to close off from outside air, and run a portable air cleaner or filter there if you have one. Wear N95 masks if available. If your central air has a fresh-air intake, set it to recirculate and close the outdoor intake damper. Keep your phone charged and keep listening to emergency alerts for instructions. Once you are out, do not return until authorities say it is safe.

question: It's 104 degrees, our AC broke, and my grandma is home with only a fan. Is the fan enough to keep her safe?
answer: No, a fan is not enough. Fans move air and feel comfortable, but they do not lower body temperature or prevent heat illness, and older adults are at greater risk in extreme heat. Get her somewhere with air conditioning today: a cooling center, a library, a shopping mall or a relative's home; your local health department can name cooling options. Until then, give her cool showers or baths, loose light-colored clothing and plenty of fluids, and check on her often. Watch for heat stroke: body temperature above 103 F, red, hot, dry skin with no sweat, a rapid strong pulse, dizziness or confusion. If you see these, call 9-1-1 or take her to a hospital immediately.

question: I'm stuck in my car on the highway in a blizzard, can't see anything. Should I walk to find help?
answer: No. Stay inside your car; walking off into a blizzard with no visibility puts you at serious risk of getting lost, hypothermia and frostbite. Put on any warm clothes and wrap up in blankets from your car kit, and use your water, snacks and flashlight. Limit any time outside the car. Keep watching yourself and any passengers for hypothermia (shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech or drowsiness) and frostbite (numbness, white or grayish-yellow, firm or waxy skin on the face, fingers or toes). If you develop these signs, warm the center of the body first. Stay put until help reaches you or the storm clears.

question: Power's been out for two days and it's freezing inside. Can I run the generator in the garage with the door open, or heat the house with the gas oven?
answer: No to both. Never run a generator inside a home or garage, even with the door open: generators and fuel must be used outdoors and at least 20 feet away from windows, doors and attached garages. Do not heat your home with a gas stove or oven either. Both can build up carbon monoxide, a colorless, odorless gas that can kill you, your family and pets; make sure you have working carbon monoxide detectors with battery backup on every level. If the cold is extreme, go to a community location with power or a warming center; check with local officials about what is open. Meanwhile layer warm clothes and blankets, keep the generator dry, and let it cool before refueling.

question: Sirens and the radio say there's a chemical leak near us and to stay indoors. How do we make the house safe?
answer: Stay inside and seal up. Bring everyone and your pets in. Close and lock all exterior doors and windows, close vents, fireplace dampers and as many interior doors as possible. Turn off air conditioners, fans and ventilation, or set ventilation to 100 percent recirculation so no outside air is drawn in. Go to an interior room and seal it with plastic sheeting and duct tape; block gaps under doors and around vents with wet towels. If vapors may have entered, take shallow breaths through a cloth or towel. Do not eat or drink anything that may be contaminated. Keep listening to the radio or TV, and do not go outdoors, even to help others, until authorities say it is safe. Some toxic chemicals have no smell.

question: Emergency alert says there was a radiation release at the nuclear plant near us and I'm outside walking home. What do I do right now?
answer: Get inside the nearest building now, do not keep walking home. Move away from windows and put as many walls as possible between you and the outside. The rule is: get inside, stay inside, stay tuned. Once inside, take off your outer layer of clothing carefully, which can remove up to 90 percent of radioactive material, bag it, and shower or wash exposed skin and hair with soap and water, or wipe them with a clean wet cloth. Close windows, doors and fireplace dampers and turn off fans and air systems that draw in outside air. Sheltering usually lasts at least 24 hours. Follow official instructions and evacuate only if officials tell you to, using the routes they give.

question: We just got an evacuation order and have maybe 20 minutes. What do we do before we leave?
answer: Grab your emergency supply kit or go-bag, medicines and your pets, and be ready to go well before the deadline; leaving early keeps you from getting trapped. If time allows: call or email your out-of-state contact and tell them where you are going; close and lock doors and windows; unplug radios, TVs and small appliances but leave the fridge and freezer plugged in unless flooding is likely; and leave a note saying when you left and where you are going. Shut off water, gas and electricity only if your home is damaged and you are told to. Wear sturdy shoes, long pants and long sleeves. Check whether neighbors need a ride, then follow the recommended evacuation route.

question: Evacuating by car and traffic is jammed. My map app says take a back-road shortcut, but there's water across that road. Should I go?
answer: No. Stay on the recommended evacuation route even if it is slow; shortcuts may be blocked, and that one is flooded. Do not drive into flooded areas: six inches of water can make a car lose control or stall, a foot of water will float many cars, and you cannot see whether the road under the water has washed out. Never drive around barricades. Also watch for washed-out roads or bridges and downed power lines. Keep a battery-powered radio on and follow local evacuation instructions, which will tell you about closures and open routes. If you are forced to stop, stay out of moving water. Turn around, don't drown.

question: If we evacuate to a public shelter for the hurricane, can we bring our dog?
answer: Take your dog with you when you evacuate, but do not count on a public shelter taking it: most public shelters allow only service animals, and many hotels do not allow pets either. All shelters do accept service animals. So plan ahead for a place that will accept your dog, such as friends or relatives outside the area or a pet-friendly hotel, and pack the dog's supplies in your go-bag. You can search for open shelters by texting SHELTER and your ZIP code to 43362 and ask whether they or nearby facilities take pets. Leaving early gives you more options if your first choice turns you away.

question: There's a strong chemical smell in our office building, people are coughing and their eyes burn. How do I get out safely?
answer: Leave now by a route that does not take you through the area where the smell is strongest. Coughing and burning eyes are signs of a chemical release. If every way out passes through the affected area, move as far away from it as you can and shelter in place in a room with the door closed. Once outside, quickly move away toward clean air, upwind of the source, and do not go back in for belongings. Tell others to do the same and call 9-1-1 for anyone having a medical emergency. If you were exposed, remove contaminated clothing, wash skin with soap and water, flush your eyes with water, and get medical screening as soon as it is safe.

question: The hurricane passed and we want to drive back home from the shelter today. What should we watch out for?
answer: First check with local officials, both where you are staying and back home, and return only when they say it is safe; going back before storm debris is cleared is dangerous. Let friends and family know when you leave and when you arrive. Fill your gas tank, charge your devices and bring water and non-perishable food. On the road, avoid downed power or utility lines, which may be live with deadly voltage, and report them to the utility. Do not drive into flooded areas, and be careful where water has receded: roads may have weakened and could collapse under a car. At home, only use a generator outside and away from the house, never inside a home or garage.

question: My friend cut his leg on broken glass and blood is spurting out. What do I do right now?
answer: Press hard directly on the wound now, with a cloth or your hand, and keep pressing; spurting bright red blood means an artery, and serious bleeding must be controlled immediately. Have someone call 9-1-1. Raise the leg above the level of the heart while you keep pressure; elevation alone will not stop it. If it keeps bleeding, put a thick pad of cloth over the wound and wrap it tightly in place as a pressure dressing. Do not remove it even when it soaks through; add more on top. Use a tourniquet only if direct pressure and everything else fail: 5 to 10 cm above the wound, between the wound and the heart, tightened just enough to stop the bleeding. Keep him lying down and warm against shock.

question: We pulled my friend out of a cold lake. He's shivering hard, slurring his words and seems confused. How do I warm him up?
answer: These are signs of hypothermia, which is an emergency: call 9-1-1. Get him to a warm room or out of the wind, remove the wet clothes and put him in dry clothing, then wrap him in warm blankets, including his head and neck. Warm the center of the body first, the chest, neck, head and groin, not the arms and legs. Rewarm him gradually: rapid rewarming, such as putting the whole body in a hot bath, belongs in a hospital because of the risk to the heart. Body heat helps: share a warmed sleeping bag or blankets with him. Do not force anyone who is unconscious or very drowsy to drink.

question: My coworker collapsed outside in the heat. His skin is red, hot and dry and he's confused. What do I do?
answer: This looks like heat stroke, a life-threatening emergency. Call 9-1-1 now, or get him to a hospital immediately. While you wait, move him into a cool, shaded area and remove his outer clothing. Cool him as fast as you can: put cold, wet cloths or ice packs on his head, neck, armpits and groin, or soak his clothing with cool water, and fan him. Elevate his feet. Red, hot, dry skin with no sweat, a fast strong pulse and confusion are the warning signs, and they mean his body can no longer control its temperature. Stay with him; he may vomit or struggle, and be ready to start CPR if he stops breathing.

question: My son's sleeve caught fire at the stove. It's out now, but his arm is red and blistering. What do I do?
answer: Cool the burn right away under cool running water, not cold water or ice, for at least three to five minutes; up to 10 to 15 minutes until it is less painful. Gently remove clothing, jewelry and anything metal from the burned area unless it is stuck to the skin. Do not break the blisters, because an opened blister can get infected, and do not put butter, oil, creams or lotions on it. Cover the burn loosely with a clean, dry cloth or a sterile non-stick dressing. Burns from a fire need medical help: call 9-1-1 or take him to the hospital. Get help especially if the burn is larger than two inches, glossy with lots of blistering, or dry and leathery.

question: After the flood our tap water is cloudy and we're out of bottled water. How do we make it safe to drink?
answer: First let the particles settle, or strain the water through coffee filters or layers of clean cloth. Then boil it, which is the safest method: bring it to a rolling boil for one full minute and let it cool; pouring it between two clean containers improves the taste. If you cannot boil, use regular unscented household liquid bleach with 5.25 to 6.0 percent sodium hypochlorite, never scented, color-safe or bleach with added cleaners. Add 1/8 teaspoon per gallon, stir and wait 30 minutes; it should smell slightly of bleach. If not, repeat and wait 15 minutes more; if it still does not smell of chlorine, discard it. Boiling and bleach kill germs but do not remove chemicals or heavy metals; only distillation does.

question: I'm lost on a hike, it's getting dark and cold, and I'll have to spend the night out here. How should I set up shelter?
answer: Start on shelter now, before full dark; in the cold, shelter can matter more than food. Pick a spot that is level enough to lie down, has materials nearby, and is not under dead trees or loose rocks that might fall. Avoid flash-flood areas, dry streambeds and ground near water below the high-water mark. Keep the shelter small: the most common mistake is building it too large, and it must be small enough to hold your body heat. If you build a lean-to with a poncho, tarp or branches, check the wind and set its back into the wind. To reduce heat loss to the ground, put insulating material such as leaves or pine needles inside your shelter.

question: After shoveling snow, two of my fingers are numb, white and waxy. Should I rub them or use a heating pad?
answer: No, do not rub them and do not use a heating pad. Numb fingers with white or grayish-yellow, firm or waxy skin are signs of frostbite. Go into a warm room now. Soak the fingers in warm (not hot) water, or warm them with body heat, for example by putting your hands under your armpits. Massaging can damage the frozen tissue, and a heating pad can burn skin you cannot feel. Do not go back out in the cold where they could refreeze: frostbite that thaws and then freezes again causes more damage. If the feeling does not come back or the skin stays hard or pale, treat it as deep frostbite and get medical care. Also watch for shivering or confusion, which mean hypothermia.

question: My toddler just drank some cleaning product from under the sink. What do I do?
answer: Call Poison Control now at 1-800-222-1222; it is free and open 24 hours a day. If your child has trouble breathing, collapses or is unconscious, call 9-1-1 instead. Follow the operator's or dispatcher's first-aid instructions carefully; the advice printed on containers may be out of date or inappropriate. Do not give your child anything by mouth, not water, milk or food, and do not try to make them vomit, unless a medical professional tells you to. While you wait, watch for difficulty breathing, irritation of the mouth or throat, changes in skin color, dizziness or clumsiness, and tell the operator if these appear.

question: When I call 911 in an emergency, what should I tell the dispatcher?
answer: Get yourself out of danger first, then call. Start with your exact location: the address or, if you are trapped, exactly where you are, and where anyone who needs help is located, for example which room a person is still in. Then say what is happening, giving full and accurate information: fire, flood, injury, how many people are hurt, and any hazards such as an attacker, their location and weapons. Full, accurate details help the dispatcher send the right responders and equipment. Answer the dispatcher's questions and follow their first-aid instructions carefully. If you are trapped, say so, and signal for help at a window with a flashlight or a light-colored cloth.

question: Help me set up a family emergency communication plan in case a disaster hits while we're all in different places.
answer: Pick one out-of-state contact everyone will check in with. Agree on meeting places if you get separated: one familiar, easy-to-find spot near home and one outside your neighborhood. Plan to text rather than call: texts need less bandwidth and get through more reliably when networks are overloaded, and save phone calls for emergencies. Keep phones charged and have a backup charger. Make sure everyone, including children, knows how and when to call 9-1-1 and has the key numbers saved and written down. Write the plan down with contacts, meeting places and medical information, give everyone a copy, and practice it together.

question: I smell gas in my house and hear a hissing sound near the stove. What do I do?
answer: Get everyone out of the house now; if a window is right next to you, open it on your way out, but do not stay to search for the leak. Do not switch lights or appliances on or off or use anything electrical inside, because electrical sparks can ignite leaking gas. Once you are a safe distance away, call 9-1-1, or call the gas company from a neighbor's home. If you know how and can reach it safely, turn off the gas at the outside main valve. If the gas is turned off for any reason, only a qualified professional can turn it back on; never do it yourself. Stay out until the fire department or gas company says it is safe.
